source.title: Detoxifying LLMs via Representation Erasure-Based Preference Optimization
source.authors: N. Sepahvand; Eleni Triantafillou; H. Larochelle; D. Precup; Daniel M. Roy; G. Dziugaite

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates recovery attacks on detoxified models and reports the resulting toxicity, using its own detoxification method and comparison methods rather than reproducing one of the original methods named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for relearning, orthogonalization, and enhanced-GCG attacks in Table 1; these are recorded below. It also reports GPT-2 Small relearning trends in Figure 3, but that figure supplies no exact values, and Table 1 already provides the attack results across two other model settings. The paper's cited claims about prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study applies the standard unlearning recovery attacks (relearning, orthogonalization, enhanced GCG, after Łucki et al.) to unlearned models in a new setting: detoxification of GPT-2 Medium and Gemma-2B. It reports how much of the removed behaviour returns, which bears on B, C, E and F. Caveat: the target is toxic generation scored by Perspective API, not factual or hazardous knowledge accuracy. It is a neighbouring construct, so these verdicts hold only for 'unlearned toxic behaviour'. A is not tested: no near-chance knowledge accuracy. D is not tested: no quantization attack.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but understated. The authors claim REPO achieves 'state-of-the-art robustness', stopping relearning and enhanced GCG where baselines fail, and that it 'consistently outperforms all baselines across attacks'. They attribute this to deep, localized, token-level representation edits and argue output-based methods are 'output suppressors'. The table does not fully back 'stopping': REPO forget-set relearning still recovers 15–32%. The text also misquotes Table 1, citing RealToxicity retain values (0.207 vs 0.245) as PairToxicity.
record.recipe_differences: REPO is a new token-level, representation-erasure preference optimization method trained with retain anchoring and a domain-adversarial objective; the study does not reproduce the original unlearning recipes named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The amount of post-attack toxicity varies by detoxification method, attack type, dataset, and model. The paper also gives differing retain-set relearning sample counts: 1000 in Section 3.2 and 100 in Appendix B.

fits_no_version.finding: REPO yields larger weight-space distances and deeper, token-localized representation drift than DPO and NPO, which give diffuse, shallow changes (Figs 4, 7, 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-space unlearning makes diffuse, low-magnitude internal edits; representation-space methods make deeper ones.

record.code_released: The paper says code will be released upon acceptance; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The attack table reports no error bars or per-run variability, although Appendix B says relearning values average three runs. The retain-set attack size is inconsistent in the text (1000 versus 100). Results measure toxicity scores, not recovery of factual knowledge. Enhanced GCG uses a reference model as a malicious teacher, which the authors acknowledge may be an unrealistic access assumption.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 reports GPT-2 Small relearning trends across subset sizes for DPO, NPO, and REPO, but exact values are not stated in the text; not extracted because Table 1 supplies the exact attack results for GPT-2 Medium and Gemma-2B.

untested.parts: No targeted-knowledge accuracy and no near-chance criterion; toxicity reduction plus MMLU utility only.
Restoration of factual or hazardous knowledge; relearning on unrelated corpora (only same-dataset forget and retain samples are used).
Mechanistic evidence of access-blocking versus deletion for the baselines; only diff-in-means orthogonalization is tested.
Rephrasing, other languages and in-context information; only white-box enhanced GCG is tested.
REPO against quantization, prompt-only attacks, and larger or instruction-tuned models.

missing.what: GPT-2 Small relearning curves over forget sizes 10–50 and retain sizes 100–500 for DPO, NPO and REPO (declared in rows_left_out; values only readable from the figure).

record.verdict_notes: States were computed as the fraction of the unlearning reduction regained: (post-attack − post-unlearning) / (reference − post-unlearning). Changes under about 0.01 were treated as absent; no error bars are reported. Rows labelled 'Relearning Forget (RealToxicity)' fine-tune on PairToxicity forget samples and evaluate on RealToxicityPrompts. The retain-set size is inconsistent: 1000 in Section 3.2, 100 in Appendix B. Gemma NPO (PairToxicity) and Gemma RMU (PairToxicity) barely reduced toxicity, so recovery there is uninterpretable. Verdicts rest on toxicity behaviour, not knowledge; downweight them if the claim is read strictly as knowledge recovery.

versions.untested_parts: It measures toxicity and utility, not targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance; it does not establish the full near-chance-and-utility condition specified by this version.
No recovery of factual knowledge is measured; the outcome is toxicity of generations. It tests relearning on forget examples and retain examples, not other kinds of unrelated or loosely related sets.

Tests an orthogonalization attack that projects out the reference-minus-unlearned activation direction; it does not test a generic single-direction ablation or establish whether the effect is deletion versus access blocking.
Tests enhanced GCG jailbreak prompting only, not rephrasing, other languages, or in-context information.
REPO is tested against the attacks used in this study; no quantization or other-language/rephrasing attack is tested.

source_check.notes: All 25 values match Table 1. In relearning rows, 'RealToxicity' is the evaluation set; fine-tuning used PairToxicity samples. Gemma DPO retain cells equal its forget cells (possible copy error). Retain-attack size: 1000 (Sec. 3.2) vs 100 (App. B). Sec. 5 prose mislabels REPO's .119/.207 against Table 1's row order. Code is only promised. REPO is the authors' own method.

statements.correction: Code: promised upon acceptance (App. B), no link given. CB GPT-2 Medium after forget-set relearning (10 PairToxicity samples, 3-run mean): 0.120 to 0.438, vs 0.281 pre-unlearning (r25).
statements.problem: Numbers right, but the 'why' credits 2602.23391 with code. The text only promises code 'upon acceptance' and gives no repository.
REPO is the study's own method; 15-32% matches r31 (20%), r33 (15%), r01 (32%), r03 (29%).

statements.correction: GPT-2 retain-set changes range from -0.018 to +0.015.
statements.problem: Minor: CB RealToxicity retain is 0.332 to 0.314 (drop 0.018), a little over 0.015; r55 is a forget-set row, not retain.
Retain samples here are benign continuations from the same dataset, so 'loosely related' is arguable.

statements.correction: Study: GPT-2 Medium RMU, mean-difference direction projected out, RealToxicity toxicity 0.363 to 0.525 (pre-unlearning 0.513) (r23). Name it in the body or drop the citation.
statements.problem: Body and conditions cover only WMDP on Zephyr and Llama. Cited r23 is RealToxicity toxicity on GPT-2 Medium RMU, so readers cannot place it.

Gemma-2B failure is for toxicity of base models, not WMDP.
